description: We’re Team USACS, a group of Rutgers students from the Undergraduate Student Alliance of Computer Scientists, the university’s largest CS club. Rohan, Tanish, Hasan, and Brayden spend the year running workshops, mentorship programs, and hackathons, so we’re used to turning ideas into something people can use. We’re excited to take on a NASA Space Apps challenge together!
summary: Tranquility Base is an interactive lunar south-pole landing site navigator that helps mission planners, educators, and the public compare candidate locations and landing dates. The application combines NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA terrain data with JPL Sun and Earth positions for 2026–2035 to visualize how local topography affects solar illumination and direct-to-Earth visibility. Users can explore terrain in 3D, inspect conditions from the surface, and evaluate mission requirements for continuous sunlight, darkness duration, Earth visibility, and slope. When a landing date changes, the constraint-based search ranks alternative locations and later dates, explains their tradeoffs, and supports side-by-side scenario comparisons. Optional natural-language input simplifies requirement entry, while shared mission rooms synchronize plans across participants. By integrating terrain, celestial geometry, mission constraints, and time within a single interface, Tranquility Base makes complex lunar environmental conditions accessible and supports informed preliminary site screening, collaborative exploration, and science education.
details:
Tranquility Base is an interactive navigator for comparing lunar south-pole landing sites and dates. Users can explore nine curated sites, enter coordinates that snap to the nearest search point, or select a location directly on the Moon view. They can set a UTC landing time for 2026–2035, move through the lunar day, and stand on the terrain in 3D. Calculated Sun and Earth positions appear against the local terrain horizon, while a panorama and readouts show illumination, geometric Earth visibility, and countdowns to sunset and Earthset. Terrain shading, a topographic layer, and contour lines provide additional geographic context.

Users define requirements for continuous sunlight, maximum darkness, Earth visibility, and slope, alongside search distance and allowable delay. When a landing plan changes, the finder evaluates alternative points and later dates, ranks results, and explains their differences from the original plan. Results can be filtered by location, delay, distance, and criteria met, then sorted by constraint margin or earliest landing. A scenario matrix, illumination and Earth-visibility layers, and comparisons of up to four scenarios help users examine tradeoffs. Planner and Explorer modes, guided tours, shareable links, and synchronized mission rooms support individual exploration and collaboration.

The principal benefit is faster, clearer preliminary site screening. Users can investigate how small changes in location or time affect sunlight and Earth visibility within one interface. Displaying the calculated horizon alongside mission metrics makes the reasons behind those changes visible. The intended impact is to make lunar planning concepts accessible to students and the public while helping mission teams explore preliminary scenarios and communicate their choices.

The project combines NASA LRO LOLA elevation data with JPL DE440 ephemeris data and NAIF lunar orientation kernels. A Python pipeline using Skyfield, NumPy, Numba, and Rasterio precomputes celestial positions and terrain horizons. A TypeScript engine calculates visibility and mission metrics locally, while a Web Worker searches alternatives without blocking the interface. React, Three.js, and react-three-fiber provide the interactive views. Cloudflare Workers host the application, R2 serves data, and Durable Objects synchronize mission rooms through WebSockets. Optional Gemini features translate written requirements and date-slip scenarios into proposed settings for users to confirm; the scientific engine computes the mission metrics.

The project’s creative contribution connects visual explanation with actionable comparison: users can see a ridge obstruct the Sun or Earth, understand the resulting constraint failure, and immediately investigate alternatives. The team considered scientific accuracy, computational performance, accessibility across experience levels, collaboration, and transparent presentation of uncertainty. Validation compares celestial angles with JPL Horizons and illumination and slope patterns with NASA reference products. The application distinguishes measured terrain from illustrative visual effects and explicitly limits its claims: its 500-metre search grid supports exploration and preliminary screening, while detailed landing hazards, power systems, thermal survival, trajectories, and communications performance require further analysis.
